Welcome to Christian Leader's Institute's Information Literacy Tutorial. Research is more than finding information. It is a process of asking useful questions, searching strategically, evaluating evidence, using sources responsibly, and communicating what you learn. This tutorial introduces practical information-literacy skills that you can apply to academic assignments, ministry research, professional questions, and lifelong learning.The goal of this tutorial is to assist you with the ability to identify the different roles information may play. You will be introduced to topics related to the location, evaluation, selection, and use of information sources, ethical source integration and citation management. Through critical thinking applications and practicing evaluation, use, and creation of information, this tutorial should get you started in helping you succeed in your coursework and assignments.

The tutorial is self-paced. Move through the modules in order when possible because later modules build on skills introduced earlier. Read the explanations, study the examples and visuals, and use the downloadable handouts in the last lessons in each module to apply the ideas to your own research.  Each module ends with one short wrap-up quiz. The practice prompts are ungraded. If you do not get an answer correct, simply review the relevant section and try again by clicking the "reset" button. 

Each self-paced module can be completed in 10-15 minutes.

  2. Responsible AI for Christian Scholars
  3. From Topic to Thesis
  4. Finding & Understanding Sources
  5. Searching Strategically
  6. Evaluating Information & Authority
  7. Writing Successful Research Papers
  8. Researching for Ministry

Quiz feedback is part of the learning process. A wrong answer is a signal to revisit the concept, not a penalty. Use the feedback, review the relevant explanation or example, and retry the wrap-up quiz when you are ready.

Module Introduction

Academic integrity is not only about avoiding punishment. It is about transparency: readers should be able to tell which ideas, words, evidence, and interpretations are yours and which came from other sources. Responsible source use also allows readers to verify evidence and follow the scholarly conversation.


Learning Objectives

By the end of this module, you should be able to:

  • Explain why researchers cite sources.
  • Recognize plagiarism and problematic source use.
  • Distinguish quotation, paraphrase, summary, and common knowledge.
  • Use note-taking practices that preserve attribution.
  • Follow the citation style required by your academic context.
  • Integrate sources without losing your own analytical voice.

Why do we cite? 

  • Credit — acknowledge the people and organizations whose work contributed to yours.
  • Traceability — help readers locate the original source.
  • Evidence — show what supports your claims.
  • Conversation — demonstrate how your work relates to existing scholarship and ideas.


Citation does not weaken your voice. Used well, it shows that your claims are grounded in evidence and that you understand the conversation you are entering.

odeComponent.htmlView:
Plagiarism includes presenting another person’s words, ideas, or work as your own. It can involve direct copying without quotation and citation, but it can also happen when a paraphrase follows the original wording or sentence structure too closely, when a distinctive idea is used without attribution, or when someone else’s work is submitted as your own.


Important
Changing a few words is not the same as paraphrasing. A true paraphrase restates the idea in genuinely new wording and sentence structure while preserving the meaning—and it still requires citation.

odeComponent.htmlView:
Quotation

  • A quotation uses the source’s exact words. Use quotation marks or the required block-quotation format and cite the source. Quote when the exact wording is especially important, distinctive, or necessary for analysis.

Paraphrase

  • A paraphrase restates a source’s idea in your own wording and structure. It should accurately preserve the meaning and must be cited because the idea still comes from the source.

Summary

  • A summary condenses a larger section or source into its main point. It is shorter and less detailed than a paraphrase, but it also requires citation when it represents a source’s ideas.

Example

Original idea: A study reports that structured reflection helped participants connect leadership theory to ministry experience.

Too close: Structured reflection helped participants connect leadership theory with ministry experience.

Better paraphrase: Participants appeared to integrate leadership concepts more effectively when the program gave them intentional opportunities to reflect on their ministry experiences (citation).

odeComponent.htmlView: Common knowledge is information that is widely known and can be found consistently across many standard sources, such as basic historical dates or broadly established facts. It often does not require citation. However, what counts as common knowledge depends on the audience and context. When a fact is specialized, disputed, surprising, statistical, or central to your argument, citation is usually the safer and more useful choice.

odeComponent.htmlView:
A source should not appear in a paragraph without a reason. One useful pattern is: introduce the source or idea, present the quotation/paraphrase/summary with a citation, and then explain why that evidence matters to your point.



Example
Research on mentoring has emphasized the importance of guided reflection. One study found that participants benefited when mentoring conversations helped them interpret ministry experiences through leadership concepts (citation). This suggests that the value of mentoring may depend not only on access to an experienced leader but also on the structure of the reflective conversation.

Try It
Take one source you plan to use. Write one sentence that introduces the idea, one paraphrase or short quotation with a citation placeholder, and one sentence explaining why the evidence matters.

Estimated time: 12–18 minutes


Module Introduction

Generative AI can help with some parts of the research process, but it can also produce inaccurate information, fabricated citations, misleading summaries, or polished answers that are difficult to verify. Responsible use begins with the rules governing your assignment and continues with verification, transparency, privacy, and personal responsibility.

Generative AI produces language by predicting plausible responses. A response can sound confident and polished while containing factual errors, invented quotations, incorrect details, or citations to sources that do not exist. This problem is often called hallucination.

odeComponent.htmlView:
If AI suggests a source or makes a factual claim, move outside the AI system. Search the library, publisher, journal, database, official source, or other appropriate resource. Confirm that the source exists, read the actual source, and check whether it supports the claim.

  1. Locate the real source.
  2. Confirm the author, title, publication, date, and other details.
  3. Read the relevant part of the original source.
  4. Check whether the source actually supports the claim.
  5. Cite the real source—not the AI-generated description of it.


Example
AI provides a convincing journal citation about mentoring. You search the library and publisher site but cannot locate the article. Do not cite it. Treat the citation as unverified and continue searching for real scholarship on the topic.

A broad topic gives you a place to begin, but it usually does not give you enough direction to begin serious research. Consider the topic mentoring. There are hundreds of possible questions related to mentoring. You could investigate mentoring in business, education, churches, leadership development, youth ministry, pastoral training, or many other settings. A broad topic is therefore a starting point—not a research question.

The same is true of a topic such as discipleship. You might investigate children, adults, new Christians, small groups, spiritual formation, online discipleship, church programs, or biblical models. Before searching deeply, decide which part of the topic you actually want to investigate.

odePagStructure.blockName: Turn Your Topic into a Research Question

odeComponent.htmlView:
A focused topic identifies the subject. A research question identifies what you want to discover about that subject. Compare “Mentoring and leadership development among emerging ministry leaders” with “How does mentoring influence leadership development among emerging ministry leaders?” The first names the subject. The second gives the research direction.

A useful research question is generally focused, researchable, open-ended, clear, and appropriate in scope. Questions beginning with how, why, what, or to what extent often invite deeper investigation, but the wording should fit the purpose of the project.


Question What Is Happening? 
How does religion affect people? Too broad. Which religion, which people, and what kind of effect?
Is pastoral burnout bad? Limited. It invites yes/no and “bad” is vague.
What is the best leadership style for every church? Problematic. “Best” is undefined and “every church” ignores context.
How does mentoring influence leadership development among emerging ministry leaders? Focused, open-ended, and researchable.

odeComponent.htmlView:
Suppose your question is “What factors contribute to burnout among pastors serving small churches?” Before researching, you might assume that poor time management is the primary cause. If you search only for information supporting that belief, you are no longer investigating the question fairly.

Instead, read credible sources and look for patterns, different perspectives, and evidence that supports, complicates, or challenges your assumptions. odeComponent.htmlView:
Once you have conducted preliminary research, you can begin developing a working thesis.

The distinction is simple: the research question asks; the thesis answers.

Example

Research Question: How does mentoring influence leadership development among emerging ministry leaders?

Working Thesis: Structured mentoring can support leadership development among emerging ministry leaders by providing guidance, opportunities for reflection, and practical learning through experienced leaders.


The thesis does not simply announce the topic. It makes a claim that the paper can develop and support. Because it is a working thesis, it can change as your evidence and analysis develop.

odePagStructure.blockName: What Makes a Strong Working Thesis?

odeComponent.htmlView:
What makes a strong working thesis? Is it: 

  • Clear — the reader understands the central claim.
  • Specific — it says more than a general statement such as “Mentoring is important.”
  • Supportable — credible evidence can develop the claim.
  • Focused — it is manageable within the assignment.
  • Responsive — it actually answers the research question.
Stage Example
Too general Mentoring is important.
Better Mentoring helps ministry leaders.
Stronger working thesis Structured mentoring can support leadership development among emerging ministry leaders by providing guidance, reflection, and opportunities for practical learning.

Scholarly sources are usually written for researchers, students, or professionals and participate in an academic conversation. They commonly identify authors, engage previous scholarship, present evidence or analysis, and provide references. Popular sources are usually written for a broader audience and may report news, explain a topic, interview people, entertain, or persuade.

Popular does not mean useless. A reputable news article may be exactly what you need for a current event, public response, or recent interview. Likewise, a scholarly article may be unnecessary if you only need a basic definition before beginning deeper research.

Primary sources provide original evidence or firsthand material. Examples include interviews, surveys, original datasets, historical documents, speeches, organizational records, and artifacts.

Secondary sources analyze, interpret, or discuss primary material or other research.

Tertiary sources organize or summarize established information and are often useful for orientation.

These labels depend partly on the research question. A denominational statement might be a primary source if you are studying what that denomination officially teaches. A scholarly article analyzing that statement would be secondary. A theological encyclopedia summarizing the broader doctrine might be tertiary.

Example
Question: How did a particular pastor describe ministry challenges during a historical period? A letter written by that pastor is primary evidence. A historian’s article interpreting the letter is secondary. An encyclopedia entry summarizing the period is tertiary.

Peer review is a scholarly quality-control process. In many academic journals, an editor sends a manuscript to subject specialists who evaluate its method, evidence, reasoning, originality, and contribution. The author may be asked to revise before publication.

Peer review is valuable, but it is not a guarantee that every claim is permanently correct. Peer-reviewed studies can have limitations, researchers can disagree, and later evidence can change understanding. Treat peer review as an important indicator of scholarly process—not a substitute for critical reading.

Ministry organizations, denominations, churches, professional associations, and practitioners can provide valuable information about their own practices, policies, experiences, and perspectives. A church training manual can tell you how that church trains volunteers. A denominational statement can document an official position. A ministry report can describe a program or present organizational data.

The limitation is scope. A single organization’s experience does not automatically establish what is true for every church or ministry. When you make broader academic claims, you may need scholarly research in addition to practitioner evidence.

You want to know how "Ministry A" structures its mentoring program. Ministry A’s handbook is direct contextual evidence. If you want to claim that this mentoring structure is effective across ministries, you need broader evidence than the handbook alone.

odePagStructure.blockName: Combine Concepts with AND and OR

odeComponent.htmlView:
Boolean operators tell many databases how terms should relate. AND usually narrows a search because records must contain both concepts. OR usually broadens a search because records may contain either synonym. Parentheses can group synonyms, and quotation marks can request an exact phrase when the database supports phrase searching.

Example Search
(mentoring OR coaching) AND ("leadership development" OR "leadership formation") AND ("emerging leaders" OR "ministry leaders")


Do not assume that more terms always create a better search. Every required concept can reduce the number of results. Start with the concepts that matter most, then adjust.

odePagStructure.blockName: When a Search Does Not Work

odeComponent.htmlView:
A search may not work if there are: 

  1. Too Many Results: Make sure to add a meaningful concept, use a more specific term, search a phrase, or apply a relevant filter. Do not narrow randomly; make each change reflect the question.
  2. Too Few Results: Remove a nonessential concept, try a broader term, add synonyms with OR, or reduce filters. Check spelling and consider whether your wording is too specialized.
  3. Irrelevant Results: Study the vocabulary in the irrelevant results. You may be using a term that has a different meaning in another field. Add a context term or replace the ambiguous word with disciplinary language.

When you encounter a claim, your first reaction may be to read the entire page closely. Sometimes a faster and more reliable first move is to leave the page and investigate it. Who created it? Do not ask only “Does this look credible?” Ask “What can I verify about the source, claim, evidence, and context?”

S — Stop

  • Pause before accepting, using, or sharing the information. Ask what you know, what you do not know, and what specifically needs verification.

I — Investigate the Source

  • Learn who created the information, what relevant expertise or role they have, what organization is behind the content, and what purpose or perspective may shape it.

F — Find Better Coverage

  • Look for independent, credible sources discussing the same claim. Better coverage may confirm the claim, challenge it, or add missing context.

T — Trace Claims to the Original

  • Follow quotations, statistics, images, and research findings back to their original source whenever possible. Then check whether the original actually supports the way the claim is being presented.

odeComponent.htmlView:
Lateral reading means opening other sources to investigate the page you are evaluating. Instead of staying inside one website and relying on its self-description, search for information about the author, organization, publication, or claim elsewhere. This is especially useful when a source is unfamiliar or when a claim is surprising, controversial, or consequential.

Example

A social post says, “A new study proves 80% of pastors will leave ministry within five years.” Instead of repeating the statistic, search for the original study. You discover that the post links to a blog, the blog cites a presentation, and the presentation refers to an older survey with a different population and wording. Tracing the claim changes what you can responsibly say.

Every source comes from a context. Authors and organizations have experiences, purposes, assumptions, values, and audiences. Perspective does not automatically make a source unusable. A denominational statement is expected to represent that denomination. An advocacy organization may provide useful data while also arguing for a position.

The task is to understand the perspective, examine the evidence, and avoid asking the source to prove more than it can support. When possible, compare coverage and evidence from multiple relevant sources.

A claim is not the same thing as evidence. Ask what evidence is offered, whether it is relevant, whether it is represented accurately, and whether the conclusion follows reasonably from it.


Weak Reasoning Pattern What It Does Simple Example
Hasty generalization Draws a broad conclusion from too little evidence Two students disliked the tutorial, so all students dislike it.
False dilemma Presents only two choices when more exist Either a church uses this model or it does not care about discipleship.
Appeal to popularity Treats popularity as proof Everyone shares this statistic, so it must be true.
Ad hominem Attacks the person instead of the argument Her evidence can be ignored because I dislike her organization.
Straw man Misrepresents a position so it is easier to attack Reducing a nuanced argument to an extreme version the author did not make.

Authority is contextual. A biblical scholar may be a strong authority for questions about textual interpretation but not for the maintenance history of a local church building. A ministry administrator may have firsthand authority about how a program operates but not necessarily about the broader scholarly evidence for its effectiveness.

Ask: What specific question am I trying to answer? What kind of expertise, experience, access, or responsibility would make someone a relevant authority for that question?

Module Introduction

A successful research paper is more than a collection of facts and quotations. Your paper should use information purposefully to investigate a question, develop an idea, engage with evidence, and communicate what you have learned. Think of research writing as a conversation: you ask a question, locate sources, compare evidence and perspectives, and use your analysis to develop and support a thesis.

  • Decode an assignment before beginning research.
  • Use sources purposefully through the BEAM framework.
  • Develop your own analytical voice while using sources.
  • Engage credible counterarguments fairly.
  • Write conclusions that synthesize findings and significance.
  • Use practical research habits that support efficient writing.

Before you search, make sure you understand what you are being asked to do. Research assignments may ask you to explain, compare, analyze, evaluate, argue, interpret, or apply. Those are different tasks and require different kinds of evidence.

Example

Example Assignment: Evaluate two approaches to discipleship using at least four scholarly sources and explain their potential strengths and limitations for ministry with young adults.

Task: Evaluate and compare
Topic: Two approaches to discipleship
Context: Ministry with young adults
Evidence: At least four scholarly sources
Analysis: Strengths and limitations


Once you decode the assignment, your searching becomes more purposeful. Instead of searching only for discipleship, you might explore small-group discipleship young adults, mentoring discipleship young adults, or spiritual formation young adults.

odeComponent.htmlView:
Finding six sources does not automatically mean you have a research paper. Ask what job each source is doing. One useful way to think about source roles is the BEAM framework: Background, Exhibit, Argument, and Method.

B — Background

Background sources help readers understand context. They may provide definitions, history, statistics, foundational concepts, or an overview. Example: a scholarly reference work explains how mentoring is commonly defined in leadership literature.

E — Exhibit

An exhibit is something you examine or analyze. It might be a biblical passage, interview, survey, ministry program, historical document, case study, or organizational data. Example: your paper analyzes the mentoring program used by a particular ministry organization.

A — Argument

Argument sources contribute ideas, interpretations, findings, or claims that you engage. You may agree, challenge, compare, or build upon them. Example: a scholar argues that relational mentoring contributes to leadership formation.

M — Method

A method source gives you a theory, framework, model, or approach that you apply. Example: you use a leadership-development model to analyze a ministry mentoring program.

odeComponent.htmlView:
BEAM is not a system for permanently labeling sources. The same mentoring article could provide a definition in one paper, function as an argument in another, or supply a model used as a method in a third. The source did not change; your use of it changed.


Example: Building a paper with BEAM

Research Question: How does mentoring influence leadership development among emerging ministry leaders?

BACKGROUND: A reference source explains mentoring and leadership-development terminology.
EXHIBIT: A ministry mentoring program provides a real-world example.
ARGUMENT: Scholarly articles present research and competing perspectives about mentoring effectiveness.
METHOD: A leadership-development model provides a framework for analyzing the program.

odeComponent.htmlView:
Research papers need sources, but sources should not take over the paper. Your job is to explain why evidence matters, how sources relate, where researchers agree or disagree, what patterns you notice, and how the evidence affects your thesis.

Source-Driven Writing
Smith states that mentoring helps develop leaders. Jones also discusses mentoring. Williams says that mentoring provides support.



Researcher-Driven Writing
Research on mentoring suggests that its contribution to leadership development extends beyond the transfer of practical knowledge. Several scholars emphasize relational support and guided reflection, suggesting that mentoring may be especially valuable when emerging leaders have opportunities to interpret ministry experiences with more experienced leaders.

odeComponent.htmlView:
Scholars may interpret evidence differently, use different methods, study different populations, define concepts differently, or reach different conclusions. Disagreement can strengthen your research because it forces you to examine conditions and limitations more carefully.

Suppose your working thesis says structured mentoring supports leadership development. Then you find credible research suggesting that poorly structured mentoring can create dependency or inconsistent outcomes. Instead of hiding that evidence, use it to refine the claim: well-structured mentoring can support leadership development when relationships include clear expectations, guided reflection, and opportunities for increasing independence.

A counterargument is a credible perspective, interpretation, or body of evidence that challenges or complicates your position. Including a counterargument does not require abandoning your thesis. It demonstrates that you understand the issue well enough to engage alternatives fairly.

  1. Present your claim.
  2. Acknowledge another credible perspective.
  3. Represent it accurately.
  4. Examine its evidence.
  5. Explain how it affects your conclusion.
Example

Claim: Structured mentoring can strengthen leadership development among emerging ministry leaders.

Counterargument: Some evidence suggests that mentoring outcomes vary significantly depending on mentor quality and program structure.

Stronger response: The variation in outcomes suggests that mentoring alone should not be treated as sufficient. Its effectiveness may depend on mentor preparation, clear expectations, reflection, and intentional program design.

The conclusion is not simply a repetition of the introduction. By the end of the paper, readers have seen your evidence and analysis. The conclusion should help them understand what the research showed and why it matters.

  • Return to the research question.
  • Restate the thesis in light of the evidence.
  • Synthesize major findings rather than listing them again.
  • Explain significance or implications.
  • Acknowledge limitations when appropriate.
  • Identify future questions when useful.
Weak Conclusion
In conclusion, mentoring is important for leadership development. This paper discussed mentoring, leadership development, and emerging leaders.

Stronger Conclusion
The evidence suggests that mentoring can contribute meaningfully to leadership development when it combines relational support with intentional reflection and opportunities for practical learning. At the same time, outcomes appear to depend on the quality and structure of the relationship. For ministry organizations, establishing a mentoring program is only the beginning; careful mentor preparation and program design may be equally important.

Estimated time: 12–18 minutes


Module Introduction

Ministry research often draws on several kinds of information at once: biblical texts, reference works, commentaries, theological scholarship, historical sources, ministry documents, and practitioner experience. Strong ministry research does not ask one source type to do every job. Instead, it matches the resource to the question and evaluates both scholarly quality and interpretive context.


Learning Objectives

By the end of this module, you should be able to:

  • Use Bible dictionaries and reference works for research orientation.
  • Select commentaries according to research purpose and context.
  • Use theological journals to engage focused scholarly conversations.
  • Evaluate open-access theological resources.
  • Use ministry and practitioner sources appropriately.
  • Represent theological perspectives accurately while practicing faithful and scholarly discernment.

odeComponent.htmlView:
Bible dictionaries, encyclopedias, atlases, and handbooks can orient you to people, places, cultural practices, historical settings, terminology, and major themes. They are especially useful early in research because they can introduce vocabulary and point toward additional sources.

Reference works are usually starting points rather than the only evidence for a substantial research paper. Use them to understand the landscape, then move into the primary text and deeper scholarship appropriate to your question.


Example

You are researching "hospitality in the New Testament." A Bible dictionary can help you understand the cultural and historical background of hospitality, identify relevant terminology, and locate passages or scholarly leads. It does not replace close reading of the biblical text or deeper scholarship on the passages you analyze.

Open access means that readers can access a resource without a subscription or paywall. It does not automatically tell you whether the source is scholarly or reliable. Some excellent peer-reviewed journals and institutional repositories are open access; some freely available material is not scholarly at all.

Evaluate open-access theological resources the same way you evaluate other sources: identify the author and publisher, investigate expertise and review process, examine citations and evidence, and determine whether the resource is appropriate for your research purpose.

Ministry organizations and practitioners can provide valuable evidence about practice. Training manuals, annual reports, denominational statements, program descriptions, sermons, interviews, and ministry publications can document what people or organizations actually do, teach, or experience.

odeComponent.htmlView:
Christian scholarship does not require choosing between faithful discernment and careful research. Responsible scholarship values truth-seeking, humility, accuracy, fairness, evidence, and honest engagement with disagreement. You can hold theological commitments while still representing other positions accurately and evaluating evidence responsibly.

Avoid searching only for sources that confirm what you already believe. Distinguish between theological commitments, interpretations, historical claims, empirical claims, and ministry-practice claims. Different kinds of claims may require different kinds of evidence.


Example

You disagree with a scholar’s interpretation of a passage. Responsible research first represents the scholar’s actual argument accurately, examines the evidence and method, and then explains your disagreement. Misrepresenting the position makes your own analysis weaker, not stronger.
